title: Sequential stage timing catalogue for cohorted latency experiments
body:
Purpose and scope:
This is a working catalogue of sequential stage residence times collected during targeted latency experiments. Goal: give a compact, reproducible mapping from request cohort -> per-stage p50/p95/p99 so engineers can quickly hypothesize which pipeline stage dominates tail for a given workload. Unlike broad e2e sampling notes, this doc records a consistent microbenchmark matrix (cohorts x cache x batch) and a short recipe for reproducing traces with trace-replay-v2.

Background/context:
We frequently see workload-dependent shifts in where the tail lives (serialization, attention, RPC egress, or post-processing). Product teams want concrete levers (cache priming, batching policy, kernel selection) that map to quantifiable tail reductions. This catalogue is intended as a quick lookup and experiment log for optimizing rollouts and incident triage.

Test matrix and instrumentation:
- Trace tool: trace-replay-v2 (branch: experiment/sequential-timing).
- Hardware: 1xA100-80GB per replica, 4-replica pool, topo: single-host multi-GPU local RPC.
- Model: rwkv-3B-quant (quantized fp16 pathway).
- Workload cohorts: short (<=64 tokens), medium (65-512 tokens), long (>512 tokens).
- Cache states: cold (no KV cached), warm (last 32 requests primed), primed (explicit prefix cached).
- Batching modes: immediate (no batch wait), micro-batch (max-wait 8ms), latency-optim (max-wait 2ms).
- Sample size: 10k requests per cell; capture full per-stage timestamps (tokenize -> embed_lookup -> forward_kernels -> kv_serialize -> rpc_egress -> post_process -> egress_send).

Key definitions used here (short):
- residence time: time spent inside a stage between its start and end tap points.
- cohort delta: difference in p95/p99 relative to the short+cold+immediate baseline.

Representative results (short cohort, cold, immediate) 
Stage                        p50   p95   p99  (ms)
-------------------------------------------------
tokenize                     1.2   2.0   3.1
embed_lookup                 0.8   1.6   2.4
forward_kernels             38.5  62.3  110.2
kv_serialize                 2.6   4.0   6.8
rpc_egress                   4.1   8.9  13.7
post_process                 1.5   3.4   6.0
egress_send                  0.9   1.8   3.0
Total E2E                  49.6  83.9  145.2

Observations: forward_kernels is the dominant p99 contributor for short cold runs (GPU compute variability and occasional micro-queue stalls cause long tails). rpc_egress contributes a persistent mid-tail (p95) due to occasional transport queuing in our local RPC pool.

Representative results (medium cohort, warm, micro-batch-8)
Stage                        p50   p95   p99  (ms)
-------------------------------------------------
tokenize                     1.8   3.0   4.5
embed_lookup                 1.0   2.2   3.4
forward_kernels             110.1 175.8  260.3
kv_serialize                 1.8   3.1   5.6
rpc_egress                   5.7  12.4  18.9
post_process                 2.3   5.1   9.7
egress_send                  1.3   2.6   4.7
Total E2E                 124.0 201.2  304.5

Notes: batching raises median and p95 predictably (forward_kernels amortized across tokens) but increases p99 when batch-formation jitter interacts with KV-miss path. Warm KV reduces kv_serialize cost and reduces some p99 mass for long outputs.

Representative results (long cohort, primed, latency-optim wait)
Stage                        p50   p95   p99  (ms)
-------------------------------------------------
tokenize                     2.6   5.9   9.2
embed_lookup                 2.0   4.8   7.6
forward_kernels             420.7 640.3  820.9
kv_serialize                 0.9   1.7   2.8
rpc_egress                  12.4  28.1  45.7
post_process                 5.1  12.3  21.5
egress_send                  3.6   7.9  13.1
Total E2E                 447.3 700.8  920.8

Interpretation patterns (catalogue entries):
- GPU compute tails: long forward_kernels p99s are caused by straggler kernel launches under high seqlen and by occasional GPU preemption events. Mitigation: prioritize fused-kernel paths, tune stream concurrency, and enable preemption-aware scheduling (ENG-1984).
- Serialization spikes: kv_serialize spikes appear when serializing large KV payloads on the same CPU thread that handles RPC. Mitigation: move serialization to worker pool, and compress small KV units.
- RPC mid-tail: rpc_egress p95 bump correlates with RPC connection churn and transport queue lengths on the host. Mitigation: connection pooling, transport backpressure, and retry budget tuning.
- Batch wait jitter: micro-batching increases median but can create a small number of long waits (p99) when the batcher holds requests waiting for a straggling client. Tuning max-wait and employ per-shard fast-lane for small tokens reduces these tails.

Repro recipe (short):
1) Checkout branch experiment/sequential-timing and run ./run/bench matrix --cohort short --cache cold --batch immediate --samples 10000 --export traces/short-cold-immediate.json
2) Load traces into trace-decomp tool: python tools/trace_decomp.py --input traces/short-cold-immediate.json --tag short-cold-immediate --out reports/short-cold-immediate.tsv
3) Use report to compute per-stage quantiles and to render stage-residence violin plots (notebook: notebooks/stage_residence_viz.ipynb).

Hypotheses to validate next (ordered):
- H1: moving kv serialization off the RPC thread reduces kv_serialize p99 by >40% and overall p99 by >8% for medium/long cohorts. (owner: Maya)
- H2: enabling fused attention kernels with stream-level concurrency reduces forward_kernels p99 for short runs by >25% without increasing median. (owner: Priya)
- H3: connection pooling for RPC clients reduces rpc_egress p95 by 30% in microburst scenarios. (owner: Ethan)

Quick action items and owners:
- Maya: prototype kv-serialize worker pool and run the medium-cohort micro-benchmark (due 2025-01-22).
- Priya: assemble fused-kernel A/B PR and add kernel-level timers (PR #893) for instrumentation (due 2025-01-29).
- Ethan: enable connection pooling and collect transport queue metrics for 48h canary (couple with production traces) (due 2025-02-05).

Known limitations and caveats:
- These numbers depend heavily on the hardware profile and process isolation. Don't transplant absolute ms values between instance types without re-running the microbenchmark.
- Our trace instrumentation currently omits GPU-side kernel split timings (we see aggregate forward_kernels). Add CUDA kernel timestamps for deeper attribution (tracked in ENG-2031).
- Network stack behavior in cloud-hosted dedicated pools may differ; validate with a dedicated-run.

Appendix: quick checklist for running a new catalogue cell
- pick cohort + cache + batch mode
- reserve a clean host with same topology
- run samples >=10k, capture full per-stage tap points
- export traces, run the trace decomp pipeline, store outputs under reports/catalogue/<cell-name>
- file a short note in this doc with the cell name, date, and top-3 dominant stages (one-liner).

Recent runs added to the catalogue:
- short-cold-immediate  (2024-11-12)  dominant: forward_kernels, rpc_egress
- medium-warm-microbatch8 (2024-12-03) dominant: forward_kernels, post_process
- long-primed-latencyopt (2025-01-11)  dominant: forward_kernels, rpc_egress

If you add new runs, append a one-line summary here (cell name, date, dominant stages) and ping #serving-runtime with the trace link.

Unresolved questions:
- Are we seeing any OS-level scheduling interference that correlates specifically with p99 forward_kernels? Need perf events and irq affinity sweeps.
- What is the crossover point (seqlen threshold) where batch amortization stops being beneficial for p99? Add a fine-grained seqlen sweep 128->1024 tokens.

Contact & ownership: eng-serving-runtime. Document author: Alexandra Kim. For questions ping @alexandra or raise ENG-1984.
